subtopic: Geometry of Complex Numbers (Argand Geometry & Loci)
title: Pitfalls & pro-tips: Argand geometry and loci

board_content.text: $e^{i\theta}$ is anticlockwise, $e^{-i\theta}$ clockwise — fix the ratio order.
The $k=1$ Apollonius locus is the perpendicular-bisector LINE, not a circle.
A fixed-argument locus is an ARC, never the full circle.
Modulus extrema on a circle are $|z_0|\pm r$ — don't guess.
Pro-tip: translate words to a $z$-equation — distance, equidistant, constant angle.
For vertex problems, reach for the rotation theorem: displacement $\times\,e^{i\theta}$.
Linearise every locus with $|w|^{2}=w\bar w$; use $|z_0|\pm r$ for extremes.

segments_english.text: Let's close the subtopic, and the chapter's teaching, with the geometry traps and the locus shortcuts.
First trap, on rotation: e to the i theta turns anticlockwise, and e to the minus i theta turns clockwise. Also mind the ratio order, since flipping it flips the sign of the angle.
Second: the Apollonius locus with k equal to one is not a circle. Equal distances give the perpendicular-bisector line. Calling it a circle is the classic mistake.
Third: a locus of constant argument is an arc, never the full circle. The other half carries the opposite angle.
Fourth: for the extremes of modulus z on a circle, the answers are the centre distance plus or minus the radius. Don't guess and don't reach for calculus.
Now the pro-tips. Translate the words into a z-equation: distance from a point becomes modulus z minus z zero; equidistant becomes a perpendicular bisector; constant angle becomes an arc.
For any vertex-finding or configuration problem, reach straight for the rotation theorem: take a displacement and multiply by e to the i theta.
And two habits to keep: linearise every locus using modulus w squared equals w times w bar, and for modulus extremes on a circle just use the centre distance plus or minus the radius.

segments_hinglish.text: Subtopic, aur chapter ki teaching, band karte hain geometry traps aur locus shortcuts ke saath.
Pehla trap, rotation par: e to the i theta anticlockwise ghoomta hai, aur e to the minus i theta clockwise. Ratio order bhi dhyaan mein rakho, kyunki use flip karna angle ka sign flip kar deta hai.
Doosra: k barabar one wala Apollonius locus circle nahi hai. Equal distances perpendicular-bisector line dete hain. Ise circle kehna classic mistake hai.
Teesra: constant argument ka locus ek arc hai, kabhi poora circle nahi. Doosra half opposite angle rakhta hai.
Chautha: circle par modulus z ke extremes ke liye, answers hain centre distance plus or minus radius. Guess mat karo aur calculus mat uthao.
Ab pro-tips. Words ko z-equation mein translate karo: kisi point se distance banti hai modulus z minus z zero; equidistant banta hai perpendicular bisector; constant angle banta hai arc.
Kisi bhi vertex-finding ya configuration problem ke liye seedha rotation theorem uthao: ek displacement lo aur e to the i theta se multiply karo.
Aur do aadatein rakho: har locus ko modulus w squared barabar w times w bar se linearise karo, aur circle par modulus extremes ke liye bas centre distance plus or minus radius use karo.
